\phantomsection\section*{Abstract}\label{sec:abstract}\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Abstract}

This thesis asks whether water and sanitation (WASH) conditions are associated with child anthropometric outcomes (height-for-age, weight-for-age and weight-for-height z-scores) in four Sub-Saharan African countries: Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya and Nigeria, selected for data availability and recency. The baseline analysis distinguishes a child's own household WASH facilities from the WASH conditions of the surrounding community; a preliminary extension links earlier DHS rounds for three of the four countries to modelled annual gridded local WASH coverage (IHME) for a defined early-life window, addressing the baseline's limitation that WASH is recorded only once, at the survey date. Both analyses are cross-sectional and observational; every estimate is a conditional association, not a causal effect.

The baseline sample pools each country's most recent DHS round (2022--2025). Household WASH, estimated with cluster fixed effects, reaches no significance at the 5\% level for any outcome (water--HAZ closest, \emph{p} = .062): inconclusive, not evidence of no association. Community WASH coverage, estimated with region fixed effects, shows a large, significant association before covariate adjustment that attenuates to non-significance once socioeconomic and region controls are added, consistent with, though not proof of, confounding by local development.

The historical extension's primary finding is the pooled established-date water--HAZ association: β = 1.03 per 10 percentage points (95\% CI {[}0.51, 1.54{]}, \emph{p} \textless{} .001), one of six nominally significant cells among 24 with no multiplicity adjustment, sensitive to the pooled weighting convention (0.41, \emph{p} = .035, unweighted), and independently reproduced with a second estimation library. The estimates are weighted conditional associations among eligible measured children, not population-representative, and carry unresolved measurement-weight documentation and other disclosed limitations.

Because the baseline and historical samples differ at once in children, survey rounds, exposure construction and controls, their contrast cannot be attributed to exposure timing; the historical result is preliminary and does not overturn the baseline conclusions. The thesis contributes a side-by-side household/community comparison and a preliminary attempt at genuine early-life exposure timing. Neither analysis identifies a causal policy effect or cost-effectiveness; the associations reported can inform research questions and interpretation, not policy recommendations.
